title: The Inside Counsel Movement, Professional Judgment and Organizational Representation
author: Robert Eli Rosen

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities or verification demands. It redirects the work-redesign question toward corporate governance, professional jurisdiction and the allocation of responsibility between inside and outside counsel, arguing that work allocation reflects fees, organisational goals, compliance commitments and professional power rather than technology alone.
qs: Corporate allocation of work between inside and outside counsel, I will suggest, is determined according to a governance structure that responds to the presence of three contractual problems.

Analysis of the proper allocation of work and responsibilities between inside and outside counsel needs to incorporate both the governance problems corporations face and the jurisdictional claims the profession supports.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source concerns inside counsel’s organisational role in shaping corporate compliance commitments, not the cluster’s proposition about converting AI capability into reliable legal services through legal engineering, verification and task-specific evaluation. Its account of organisational participation is potentially relevant by analogy, but it provides no direct position on AI implementation or service delivery.
qs: The allocation of this work to inside counsel derives from not only their access to corporate lines of communication, but also their understanding of the corporation's levels of commitment to legal compliance and their involve- ment in the processes by which these commitments are formed and changed.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: Rosen accepts that corporate legal departments shift control toward informed buyers while combining insourcing with continued use and management of outside counsel. He materially extends the cluster by explaining that this allocation reflects conditional make-or-buy economics and by framing buyer authority as power to shape corporate goals, carrying corresponding professional and organizational responsibilities.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: Rosen accepts the cluster’s core tension: in-house integration gives lawyers meaningful corporate influence but creates persistent risks of professional capture. He materially develops the proposition by rejecting organisational independence as a sufficient safeguard and proposing context-sensitive, durable duties linking inside and outside counsel.

st.t: Legal specialization: Client relationships fragment expertise
st.an: The source accepts that specialization can fragment legal work but argues that the decisive issue is organizational coordination rather than specialization itself. It materially develops the cluster by identifying corporate legal departments as integrators of outside specialists and by proposing capacity-sensitive allocation of authority and responsibility.
qs: Chief Justice Rehnquist's concern with the specialization of elite firm practitioners needs to be balanced by attention to the integrative capacities of powerful corporate legal departments.
I do assume that the outcomes ought to depend on the capacities of the client, legal department, and the elite firm.

st.t: Professional independence: Regulation should follow client vulnerability
st.an: The source accepts that professional independence and ethical performance depend on organizational conditions rather than automatically following from market success or a particular practice setting. It materially extends the cluster’s proposition by specifying governance reforms for corporate representation: inside counsel need real decisionmaking authority, while outside counsel owe duties to the organization rather than merely to the legal department.
qs: And for this work to be done properly, inside counsel need the power to mobilize corporate decisionmaking processes and to negotiate about the trade-offs between legal compliance and corporate goals.
But outside counsel's duties are to serve the organization, not inside counsel.

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: The source supports the proposition that inside counsel have gained strategic and managerial authority while remaining professional legal advisers rather than simply business managers. It also appropriately qualifies the transformation by distinguishing expanded organisational involvement from genuinely novel legal work.
qs: 199 Corporations cede to lawyers supervisory and managerial responsibilities for their legal function." They include lawyers in the groups choosing their strategic plans.
They ought not seek lawyers willing to doff their professional "hats" for business ones.' They need high quality lawyers whose advice improves with organizational involvement.

st.t: Market reform: Information and incentives shape access
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by distinguishing provider overwork from clients’ demand for unnecessarily premium services, showing that costs depend on information, purchasing choices and service intensity rather than provider numbers alone. It also recognizes a countervailing professional safeguard against cost controls that improperly curtail services, reinforcing the cluster’s context-specific treatment of incentives and protections.

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of legal work as a contested jurisdiction shaped by professional authority, organisational structures and competing occupational identities. Its inside-counsel example shows that control of legal work depends on continued professional backing and may be challenged by managerial identification or non-lawyer substitution; these are conceptual possibilities rather than measured AI effects.
qs: If the Inside Counsel Movement's jurisdictional claims are to be main- tained, support from the profession will be needed.
And non-lawyer legal consultants might substitute for inside counsel.

kp.k: In-house expansion raises questions about professional power
kp.d: This historical article does not discuss AI. Rosen examines claims that inside counsel have gained corporate power and professional prestige, asking whether and how their influence over corporate goals constitutes honorable legal service. He provisionally assumes improved professional standing to evaluate the movement's own justification, rather than treating its success or ethical superiority as established findings.
qs: Inside counsel's claims to professional standing challenge the profession to confront the political role of professional judgment in serving corporate clients.
I pose the question, even if inside counsel acted as they claim, ought they be praised?

kp.k: Growth reports require substantial empirical qualification
kp.d: Rosen contrasts selective legal-department surveys and press accounts with broader American Bar Foundation data. A cited study of a select 183 corporations reported average growth of 29% between 1977 and 1982. Broader data showed lawyers in private industry increasing by 40% between 1970 and 1980 against 53% growth for the profession overall, with private industry's share at 10% in 1960, 11% in 1970, 10% in 1980 and 9.7% in 1985. These broader figures are imperfect measures of legal-department employment because they include lawyers working elsewhere within companies. Unidentified interview quotations come from Rosen's research on six major manufacturing companies, reported in his 1984 dissertation.
qs: Lawyers reported as working in private industry include lawyers who do not work for corporate legal departments.
Nevertheless, the size of the corporate legal departments of significant clients of elite law firms may have been growing.

kp.k: Market restructuring is contingent, not inevitable
kp.d: Rosen rejects accounts portraying in-house expansion as an inevitable rationalization of legal services. Outside firms could change fees, services and organizational relationships; corporate fortunes or management philosophies could weaken legal departments; and the profession could reshape its market. He interprets the Inside Counsel Movement, including the American Corporate Counsel Association, as professional mobilization whose claims may be self-interested, rather than neutral evidence of inevitable progress.
qs: Many different structures can fulfill required functions.
Outside counsel may respond to the competition of corporate legal departments by varying their services and fee structures.
A political analysis underscores that participant observations may be self-interested.

kp.k: Organizational independence does not establish ethical superiority
kp.d: Rosen rejects both automatic deference to independent law-firm practice and automatic confidence in employed lawyers. Organizational independence may buffer professional decisions, but its ethical significance depends on professional socialization, client relationships, market conditions and organizational context. He calls for detailed investigation of actual work and decision conditions rather than judging ethics from employment form alone.
qs: Inside counsel's claims cannot be dismissed simply because they do not practice under conditions of organizational independence.
Understanding lawyers' ethical autonomy from clients requires detailed study both of what lawyers do and under what conditions they make these choices.

kp.k: In-house work combines substitution, purchasing and preventive practice
kp.d: Rosen identifies three functions: performing work otherwise assigned to outside firms; selecting, organizing, monitoring and auditing outside counsel; and organizing, monitoring and auditing corporate operations through preventive law. His make-or-buy analysis assumes that corporate governance arrangements respond to contracting problems involving fees, representation objectives and compliance commitments. This is an analytical assumption about corporate needs, not proof of social efficiency or a comprehensive empirical account of allocation decisions.
qs: The work of inside counsel at the largest corporations has three clearly discernable elements.
Nor are there any extensive empirical studies of these decisions.
I do not claim that what corporations find efficient is socially or professionally desirable or efficient.

kp.k: Costs and asset specificity influence work allocation
kp.d: Rosen argues that routine work can move inside when elite firms retain reputation-based price premiums, while client-specific work can move inside to preserve knowledge and reduce dependence on rehiring particular outside lawyers. However, internal capacity brings salary, overhead and utilization costs. Outside firms retain advantages for innovative work reusable across clients, infrequently needed specialties and demand peaks. Some work depends on irreplaceable personal expertise; third-party assurance may require an independently established reputation that inside counsel cannot provide.
qs: The delivery of legal services requires and creates client-specific assets.
When work is neither routine nor idiosyncratic, cost controls do not necessarily favor using inside counsel.
This inventory is extremely perishable. It has no shelf life.

kp.k: Budgeting governs strategy, not simply legal expenditure
kp.d: Rosen distinguishes reports of outside-firm overbilling from the broader functions of legal budgeting. Budget negotiations establish inside counsel's managerial authority, define scope and strategy, promote communication and authorize subsequent changes. He points to largely ex ante budgeting, continued reliance on hourly fees, expected overruns and relationship selection as reasons not to interpret budgeting solely as protection against supplier opportunism. Excessive work may also reflect professional commitments to precision rather than greed.
qs: The budgeting process serves to establish a relation in which outside counsel understand that inside counsel is their "client."
Inside counsel become "the client" of outside counsel in response to the difficulties of transmitting corporate interests to outside counsel.

kp.k: Legal-service management helps create corporate objectives
kp.d: Rosen argues that inside counsel are not merely inexpensive translators or information conduits. By filtering information, choosing questions, organizing contacts and prompting decisions across organizational boundaries, they influence which corporate goals emerge. Corporate fragmentation and the uncertainty of legal problems help explain why corporations need lawyers with managerial power, rather than assuming objectives are already settled and only require execution.
qs: But, they are not just translators. They are managers.
Inside counsel gain corporate power because of the uncertainties in determining the corporation's legal interests.
With the emergence of corporate legal departments, client goals are discovered that are different from those that would have emerged in their absence.

kp.k: Preventive law negotiates contested compliance commitments
kp.d: Rosen distinguishes routine implementation by technical specialists from lawyers' involvement when corporate commitments become contested. He describes three approaches: integrating compliance into incentives and procedures, educating managers while preserving discretion, and providing counsel at decision points. The choice depends on organizational needs and risk attitudes, not technical legal interpretation alone. Effective preventive practice requires influence and collaboration rather than merely vetoing illegalities; Rosen explicitly leaves open the risks of co-optation and inadequate professional performance.
qs: Lawyers are involved in preventive law practice when corporate commitments become contestable.
Inside counsel are not policemen.
What is required from the lawyer is the ability to convince others about what is in their own and the corporate interest.

kp.k: The movement claims jurisdiction over mixed business decisions
kp.d: Rosen interprets the movement as claiming that influential corporate counseling belongs within legal practice, rather than requiring lawyers to abandon professional identity for management. Managing legal services and preventive programs entails shaping policies, objectives and resource commitments. He argues that the profession must explicitly support or reject this jurisdictional claim, taking account of reported corporate demand and competition from other professional groups. Increased prestige alone cannot resolve the ethical responsibilities attached to corporate power.
qs: Inside counsel are not to be understood, the Inside Counsel Movement claims, as half lawyers/half businessmen.
The Inside Counsel Movement thus challenges the profession to take a side on whether lawyers ought to be "influential and independent counselors."
The profession must battle for corporate power both collectively and through the actions of its members.

kp.d: Addressing the Model Rules and accompanying commentary available in 1989, Rosen criticizes interpretations that make formal hierarchy the source of corporate decisions and the ceiling on lawyers' legitimate intervention. He argues that authority and objectives are dynamically negotiated, and that mandatory reliance on hierarchical review can undermine effective counseling. He recommends permitting consensually negotiated responsibilities while protecting corporate accountability, information flows and decisionmaking capacity, rather than simply preserving reporting lines.
qs: Furthermore, in defining how client decisions are ascertained, the Rule relies on a hierarchical chain-of-command that bears little relation to the dynamics of large organizations.
Rule 1.13 speaks as if lawyers had no corporate power.
Lawyers ought to serve organizations as they and their clients agree, not only as enforcers of the corporate hierarchy when agents exceed their authority.

kp.k: Outside counsel must serve corporations, not legal departments
kp.d: Rosen warns that treating inside counsel as the client can insulate legal departments from accountability. He describes possible distortions from settlement incentives, restricted information and use of outside firms to absorb blame or conceal internal mistakes. His proposed additions to Rule 1.13 would require reasonable efforts to ensure professionally compliant organizational legal work and qualified responsibility for another lawyer's violations on shared matters. These are proposed safeguards, not statements of adopted rules.
qs: But outside counsel's duties are to serve the organization, not inside counsel.
Norms must emerge to coordinate the work of inside and outside counsel so that outside counsel continue to serve the corporation as an entity, not the legal department.
A lawyer who provides services to an organization is bound by the rules of professional conduct notwithstanding that the lawyer acted at the direction of another person.

kp.k: Limited engagements require accountability across the division of labor
kp.d: Rosen argues that dividing tasks and accepting narrowly scoped assignments does not remove ethical questions about who determines objectives, supplies facts and assumes responsibility. Outside counsel should examine both restrictions on their own work and inside counsel's capacity to integrate it responsibly. Acceptable arrangements may differ across organizations; he does not prescribe one outcome for every engagement. He acknowledges that stronger reciprocal monitoring would impose costs but considers those potentially justified by professional client-service standards.
qs: What the adoption of these provisions does affect is the ability of lawyers to limit their responsibilities.
I do not assume that ethical demands force negotiation about these questions to reach only one set of outcomes.
I do assume that the outcomes ought to depend on the capacities of the client, legal department, and the elite firm.

kp.k: Specialization requires integration and deliberately sustained professional norms
kp.d: Rosen challenges treating specialization itself as the explanation for professional decline. Its consequences depend on how differentiated work is integrated, including through powerful corporate legal departments. He argues that market-generated relationships need not preserve ethical service, professional influence or the bar's public functions. His conclusion calls for explicit rights, duties and professional judgments governing the use—and failure to use—organizational power.
qs: Analysis of specialization ought to direct attention to the division of labor in which specialized services are but one part.
Professionalism is a challenge, not the natural result of market forces.
Their challenge reminds us that professionalism demands not only the study of the frailties of temptation, but also the study of the possibilities for political power.
